summary:
Mars Scout is a hyperlocal, layered explorer for planning human surface work on Mars. It combines HiRISE terrain (1 m DTM), CRISM mineral detections, a geologic map and THEMIS thermal data in one interactive 3D viewer, so a crew can see a site the way they would walk it. Most existing maps are built for regional and global views; ours is built for a single excursion.

The tool has two planning modes. Route Planning finds an optimal walking route through the area’s mineral hotspots, balancing terrain difficulty with sun and weather conditions by time of day. Build Potential ranks locations for a base or habitat using terrain suitability, nearby mineral resources and weather.

Every layer is labeled with its resolution and confidence, so a crew can tell measured data from inferred. Coarse layers explain why a region matters, while fine layers decide the actual route. Mineral detections from orbit are shown as candidates, not confirmed findings.

The goal is simple: show an astronaut where it is safe to walk, where the science is, and where it is best to build. Our prototype is built on the Jezero crater region
details:
Overview. Mars Scout is an interactive 3D explorer for hyperlocal planning on Mars. Existing tools such as Mars Trek and the USGS maps are built for regional and global views. Ours is built for the scale of a single excursion: a 21 km by 21 km site, walked at ground level. It was developed for the Jezero crater region.

Mode 1: Route Planning. The user picks a start point and the tool finds an optimal walking route through the CRISM mineral hotspots in the area. The route cost combines slope and terrain difficulty from the HiRISE 1 m DTM, sun and shadow, and weather (temperature, wind, dust) by time of day. It also checks the return path back to the start, so the crew can see whether a stop is still within a safe walk-back.

Mode 2: Build Potential. The tool scores candidate base or habitat locations using slope and terrain suitability, proximity to mineral resources, and weather conditions, and ranks the best candidates.

Layers and data.

  • Topography and imagery: HiRISE 1 m DTM and orthoimage (MRO)
  • Spectral: CRISM summary-parameter products (MRO), clipped to the site
  • Geology: USGS/JPL geologic map of Jezero crater [edit to the map you used]
  • Thermal: THEMIS thermal data (Mars Odyssey)
  • Weather: [Perseverance MEDA / modeled placeholder values, whichever you used]

Scale-aware design. Every layer is labeled with its resolution and confidence. Coarse layers explain why a region matters, and fine layers decide the actual route. CRISM mineral detections and thermal results are shown as candidates, not confirmed findings, because orbital spectra can only see surface materials and are affected by dust and mixing. This lets a crew tell measured data from inferred data.

Why it matters. A crew on Mars will need to know three things before leaving the lander: where it is safe to walk, where the science is, and where it is best to build. Mars Scout puts those answers in one view, at the scale of a real walk.

Interface. A global map-pick stage lets the user choose an area, and a first-person walking character lets them see the terrain at ground level. [Edit this to what your demo really shows.]

Tools. Python, rasterio (CRISM clipping and data processing), Three.js and Vite (3D viewer), Cloudflare R2 (tile hosting), Netlify (web hosting).

Limitations and next steps. Our prototype covers the Jezero site. Next steps are additional sites, ice-prospecting evidence tiers, and a line-of-sight communications viewshed.

AI use. Parts of the code and text were written with AI assistance (Claude).
